slots.text: Most founders skip validation because they think they already know their users. Then spend 6 months building something nobody wants.

Three things that kill user interviews:

1. Leading questions that confirm your bias
2. Talking to friends who won't tell you the truth
3. Asking what people want instead of what they actually do
The AI tools everyone's hyping don't solve the real problem: most workflows break because of human handoffs, not technical bottlenecks. Adding AI to a broken process just makes it break faster.
Founders who validate ideas by building prototypes learn slower than founders who validate ideas by having conversations. Code feels productive but conversations are efficient.
Friction isn't always bad. Sometimes the friction IS the feature that makes people value what you're building.

Signs your idea validation is actually just confirmation bias:

1. You only talk to people who already agree with you
2. You explain the problem instead of asking about it
3. You count polite interest as real demand
Most founders ask users what they want instead of watching what they actually do. The gap between intention and behavior is where real insights live.

Three signs your idea validation is going sideways:
1. Everyone says it's a great idea
2. No one asks about pricing
3. Users describe solutions, not problems

When validation feels too easy, dig deeper.

Been thinking about why AI tools feel clunky in most workflows. The problem isn't the AI - it's that we're bolting intelligence onto broken processes instead of rebuilding the process around what AI does well.

Noticed something: founders who build internal tools first tend to nail product-market fit faster. They've already lived through the pain of bad tooling and know what good friction removal actually looks like.
User interviews aren't about validating your solution. They're about invalidating your assumptions fast enough that you don't waste months building the wrong thing.

The hardest part about removing friction isn't technical - it's convincing people to change their habits. Even when your solution is objectively better, switching costs feel higher than staying stuck.
Most founders skip validation because they're afraid of hearing "no." But "no" with reasons is infinitely more valuable than "maybe" from people being polite.

Three things that make user interviews actually useful:

1. Ask about past behavior, not future intentions
2. Focus on the problem, not your solution
3. Let awkward silences happen - that's where real insights live

The hardest part of building with AI isn't the tech - it's figuring out where humans actually want to be removed from the loop vs where they want to stay in control. Most builders guess wrong on this.
Workflow friction usually isn't about the number of steps. It's about context switching between different mental models in the same process.
Good validation feels uncomfortable. You're constantly discovering that your assumptions were wrong. If validation feels confirming, you're doing it wrong.

Every founder thinks their users want more features. But when you actually watch them work, they're usually trying to avoid half the features you already built. The gap between what people say and what they do is massive.
Most founders think user interviews are about asking what people want. They're actually about watching what people do when they think nobody's looking.

Three things that kill idea validation:
1. Asking leading questions
2. Talking to friends who want to be supportive
3. Confusing politeness for product-market fit

The hardest part of building with AI isn't the tech. It's figuring out which human decisions you actually want to automate vs which ones people need to keep control over. Get this wrong and your "helpful" feature becomes deeply annoying.
When you remove one step from a workflow, users immediately find three new steps to complicate it. Friction doesn't disappear, it just moves around.
Your idea isn't validated until someone pays for it. Everything before payment is just expensive market research.

Signs you're talking to the wrong users:
1. They have unlimited budgets
2. They say everything sounds "interesting"
3. They want to schedule another call to "explore synergies"
4. They ask if you do consulting
Most founders skip user interviews because they're afraid of hearing their idea sucks. But the ones who actually suck are the ideas you never validate, not the ones you kill early.

Three things that make user interviews worthless:

1. Leading questions that confirm what you want to hear
2. Talking to people who will never pay for anything
3. Asking what they want instead of what they actually do

The hardest part about building with AI isn't the technical integration. It's figuring out which manual tasks actually deserve to be automated vs which ones give you critical business insight when done by hand.

Founders who obsess over removing friction often remove the wrong friction. They'll spend weeks perfecting onboarding flow while ignoring the fact that their core value prop takes 20 clicks to access.
Every workflow optimization reveals two new bottlenecks. The goal isn't to eliminate all friction—it's to move friction away from the parts that matter most to users.

Signs your idea validation is actually just confirmation bias:

1. Everyone you talk to loves it
2. No one mentions price as a concern
3. You haven't heard a single use case you didn't think of
4. Zero pushback on your timeline
Most founders skip the boring part of validation: actually counting how many people said yes vs how many you talked to. The ratio tells you everything the enthusiasm doesn't.

Three things that kill user interviews:

1. Leading questions that confirm what you want to hear
2. Talking to people who are too polite to tell you the truth
3. Asking about hypotheticals instead of past behavior
Teams building AI features spend 80% of their time on data pipelines and 20% on the actual AI. Then wonder why their AI demo feels bolted on instead of native.
The friction isn't usually in your product. It's in getting people to change their current workflow to use your product. They'd rather stick with their broken spreadsheet than learn something new.
User feedback falls into two buckets: things they say they want, and things they actually pay for. The second bucket is much smaller and way more valuable.

Signs your idea validation is working:

1. People interrupt you to ask pricing
2. They introduce you to their boss without prompting
3. They ask when they can start using it
4. They offer to pay upfront
Most founders skip validation because they think they already know their users. Then they build features nobody asked for and wonder why adoption is flat.

3 things that kill user interviews:
1. Leading questions that confirm your bias
2. Talking to people who will never pay
3. Asking what they want instead of what they struggle with
The AI integration paradox: users want the magic but don't trust the black box. They need to see how it works to feel confident, but showing the complexity kills the magic.
Founders who obsess over workflow optimization spend more time building systems than actually doing the work. Seen this pattern in my own habits too many times.
User feedback that starts with 'It would be cool if...' is usually worthless. User feedback that starts with 'I waste 2 hours every week because...' is gold.

4 signs you're removing real friction:
1. Users mention the pain unprompted
2. They're already using broken workarounds
3. They'll pay before you ask
4. Competitors ignore it because it's 'unsexy'
